transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit embarrassing, to be perfectly honest with you. I've been helping out at the community center for, oh, must be going on fifteen years now. Ever since I retired. I usually help set up for the Friday luncheons, you know, making sure the chairs are out, the tables are wiped down, that sort of thing. I like things done a certain way, sure, but I've always prided myself on being a patient man. I mean, at seventy-nine, you learn not to sweat the small stuff, right? But last week... well, last week, we had this new volunteer, a young kid, maybe seventeen or eighteen, doing his community service hours for high school. Good kid, really, but he was rushing. He threw a tablecloth over one of the main tables, and it was completely crooked. Hanging off one side, barely covering the other. And I just... I don't even know what came over me. I just blew up at him. I mean, I really let him have it. I raised my voice, told him he was careless, asked him if he had eyes in his head... I made a whole scene right there in the middle of the hall. The poor kid looked terrified, and everyone just stopped and stared at me. I had to go sit in my car for twenty minutes just to stop shaking. And that's... that's why I'm here. Because I don't usually talk to people that way. It's just not who I am, and it scared me, quite frankly, how fast I lost my temper over something so stupid as a piece of cloth.
Have you had any other episodes like that since the one at the community center?

Well, no, not quite like that, thank the Lord. Because, like I was just telling you, that whole thing with the tablecloth... that's the entire reason I picked up the phone and made this appointment in the first place. I mean, blowing up at one of the younger volunteers like that, it just... it doesn't make a lick of sense to me. I've been sitting in my armchair all week just stewing on it, replaying the whole thing over and over in my head. I keep asking myself where all that anger came from, you know? 

Because I don't usually talk to people that way! I really don't. You could ask anyone who knows me. I was a mail carrier for forty years before I retired, and you deal with all sorts of folks doing that—cranky dogs, bad weather, people complaining about bills—and I never once lost my cool. I was always the one to just smile and tip my hat. So for me to just explode over a piece of cheap white linen being a few inches off-center... it's ridiculous, isn't it? 

So, to answer your question, I haven't shouted at anyone else since last Friday, no. I've been a little... I don't know, maybe a bit grumpy with myself, just muttering under my breath around the house, but no big blow-ups. I've mostly just been terrified of it happening again. I keep seeing that poor boy's face, how his eyes got all wide and scared when I started raising my voice and pointing my finger at him. It's just not who I am, doctor. I'm a quiet man. I like my routines. I just can't wrap my head around why I got so aggressive out of nowhere.
Do you often find yourself thinking about details or making sure things are done in a specific way?

Well, sure, I suppose I do. But not in a... not in a bad way, you know? Just... well, like I mentioned when I first sat down, I do like things done a certain way. I think when you get to be my age, you just settle into your routines. You figure out the best, most efficient way to do a thing, and you stick to it. 

It goes all the way back to when I was carrying the mail, really. You had to be organized for that job. You sort the letters just so, you bundle the magazines, you plan your route so you're not walking back and forth across the same street wasting time and wearing out your knees. It's just common sense, being organized. And I guess I just brought all that right into my retirement. I have my morning coffee—always at six-thirty, always in the same blue ceramic mug—and then I read the paper, front to back. And at the community center, yes, I like the chairs lined up straight and the tables wiped down properly because it looks nice for the folks coming in. It shows a little respect for the people we're serving. 

So, I do pay attention to the details, yes. I like things neat and tidy. My late wife used to tease me about it, she’d say I was more stubborn than a mule in mud about my little routines. But it’s never been a problem before! That’s the thing I keep coming back to. I’ve always been particular, sure, but I never yelled at anybody over it. If a chair was crooked, or if someone put the forks on the wrong side of the plate, I’d just quietly walk over and fix it myself. I wouldn't scream at a teenager. I wouldn't make a spectacle of myself. That's why that whole business with the tablecloth just keeps eating at me. It’s like, why couldn't I just walk over and straighten the cloth myself like I normally would have done any other Friday for the last fifteen years?
Does thinking about things not being done your way cause you a lot of anxiety or stress?

Well... no, I wouldn't say it causes me anxiety. Not stress, either, really. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting around wringing my hands or pacing the floor if the forks are on the wrong side of the plate, you know? Like I said, if something's not quite right, my usual response is just to fix it. It's just a mild annoyance, maybe? Like a little itch you just have to scratch. 

For instance, my neighbor, Frank—he's a good guy, means well, but he borrows my lawn tools sometimes. And when he brings them back, he never puts them back exactly where he found them in my shed. I have the rakes on the left, the shovels on the right, and the hand tools on the pegboard. Frank will just lean the rake against the workbench. Now, does it keep me up at night? Heavens, no. Does it make my heart race or my palms sweat? Not at all. I just walk out there, pick up the rake, and put it on its hook. Takes two seconds. I might mutter to myself about Frank being a little scatterbrained, but it doesn't ruin my day. It's just... it's just a preference, doctor. I like order. I think the world runs better when there's a place for everything and everything's in its place. 

So, no, I don't get stressed out about it. It's just a part of who I am. That's what makes this whole tablecloth incident so baffling to me! Because if it doesn't normally bother me enough to raise my blood pressure even a tick, why on earth did I practically take that poor boy's head off over it? It's like... it's like a switch flipped in my brain, and I just bypassed my normal, calm reaction and went straight to yelling. And I haven't been able to stop thinking about that, trying to figure out where that came from. Because it certainly wasn't from me just being a bit particular about how the tables look.
Have you ever had any similar episodes of losing your temper before the incident at the community center?

Well, no, not really. That's... that's exactly what I've been trying to say, doctor. I mean, I really haven't. That's the whole reason I'm sitting here in this office today. Like I was telling you earlier, what brought me in is that I blew up at one of the younger volunteers over a crooked tablecloth, and I just... I don't usually talk to people that way! I really don't. 

I've been trying to rack my brain, you know, sitting in my chair at home, looking out the window, just thinking back over the years. I mean, sure, I've gotten frustrated before. Who hasn't? When I was carrying the mail, there was this one dog on Elm Street—a little terrier mix, nasty piece of work—that used to nip at my heels every single Tuesday. And yeah, I'd yell "git!" and wave my bag at him. Or maybe I'd grumble if my wife, God rest her soul, shrank one of my good wool sweaters in the wash. But that's just normal frustration, isn't it? That's not losing your temper. That's not screaming and pointing fingers and making a spectacle of yourself in front of a room full of people. 

I just... I can't think of a single time in my seventy-nine years where I lost control like that. Not with my kids when they were teenagers and testing every boundary under the sun, not with my supervisors at the post office when they tried to change my route after twenty years, not with anybody. I've always prided myself on being a level-headed man. A steady man. You have to be, when you're out in the community every day, representing the postal service. You can't just fly off the handle because someone's mailbox is blocked by a snowdrift. You just write it down, keep walking, and deal with it calmly. 

So to answer your question, no. Never. That's why this tablecloth business is so upsetting to me. It's completely out of character. It's like I was watching someone else wearing my skin, yelling at that poor boy. I just don't understand where all that anger came from, because it certainly isn't a habit of mine.
Do you find that making sure everything is done just right takes up a significant amount of your time?

Well, now, let me think on that... no. No, I really wouldn't say that at all. In fact, I'd argue it's quite the opposite! You see, when you've got a proper system in place, it actually saves you time. That’s something you learn early on carrying the mail. Efficiency is the whole name of the game. If you sort your bundle right the first time, you aren't standing out there on the sidewalk in the freezing cold fumbling through envelopes looking for Mrs. Gable's electric bill, you know? 

So, my little routines... they don't take up my day. My morning coffee, for example. I know exactly how long it takes to brew, and while it's doing its business, I've already got my blue mug out, the spoon resting right beside it, the paper folded to the local news. It’s a well-oiled machine. And down at the community center, if I see a chair pushed out of line, I just give it a little tap with my knee as I walk past. Just a quick nudge. Takes half a second. It's not like I'm down on my hands and knees with a tape measure and a level, making sure everything is mathematically perfect! 

I mean, I've got better things to do with my retirement than spend hours organizing forks or straightening rugs. I like to read, I like to watch the birds out by the feeder... So no, it doesn't eat up my time at all. It's just a quick fix here and there as I go about my day. Which, again, doctor, is exactly why this whole thing with the tablecloth is so baffling to me! If I had just reached over and given the fabric a little tug, it would have taken two seconds. Two seconds! And the table would have been perfectly straight. Instead, I stood there and wasted everybody's time, making a total fool of myself yelling at that young man. It just... it defies all logic, it really does.
Have you ever felt like you couldn't leave the house or go to bed until everything was in its perfect place?

Well, no, doctor. No, I can't say I've ever felt trapped like that. Like I couldn't go to bed? Goodness, no. When I'm tired, I go to sleep. 

Now, I do have my evening routine, sure. Like I was saying earlier about efficiency... you set yourself up for the next day. So, before I turn in, I'll make sure the front door is locked—deadbolt and the chain, just a habit from living in the neighborhood all these years—and I'll turn the thermostat down to 65, because there's no sense paying to heat a house when you're under a good heavy quilt. And maybe I'll make sure my slippers are right there at the foot of the bed, pointing outward, so I can just step right into them if I need to use the washroom in the middle of the night. At my age, you know, you don't want to be stumbling around in the dark stubbing your toe on the cedar chest. 

But if, say, I forgot to put the slippers there? Or if there was a spoon left in the sink from a late-night bowl of butter pecan ice cream? I wouldn't lose a wink of sleep over it. I certainly wouldn't get out of a warm bed to go fix it. It'll be there in the morning. 

And it's the exact same thing with leaving the house. When I worked the route, I had to be out the door by 5:30 AM sharp. Rain, sleet, snow, you name it, the mail doesn't wait. If I had to stop and make sure every little knickknack on the mantelpiece was perfectly aligned before I could walk out the front door, I would've been fired my very first year! You just grab your coat, make sure you have your keys in your right pocket, and you go. 

So, no, I don't get stuck like that. I like things tidy, yes, but I run my house, my house doesn't run me. Which is exactly why... well, you see where I'm going with this, doctor. It just brings us right back around to that community center. If I'm so sensible about everything else, if I can leave a dish in the sink and sleep like a baby, why on earth did I lose my mind over a piece of linen on a folding table? I just... I keep replaying it in my head, sitting in my armchair, and it makes absolutely no sense. I wasn't stuck, I wasn't forced to fix it, I just... exploded. And I can't for the life of me figure out why.
Do you feel a strong need to control your environment or the people around you?

Control? Well, now, that's a strong word, doctor. I wouldn't say that. No, I wouldn't say that at all. 

I mean, sure, I like my own personal things a certain way, like I told you about my coffee mug and my slippers, but other people? The rest of the world? Lord, no. You can't control other people. If I've learned anything in seventy-nine years on this earth, it's that folks are going to do exactly what they want to do, when they want to do it, and you'll just give yourself a heart attack trying to stop them. 

Take my neighbor, Bill, for instance. Bill leaves his trash cans out on the curb until Thursday sometimes. Now, trash pickup is Tuesday morning! Does it bother me a little bit to look out my front window and see those big green plastic bins sitting there for two extra days? Maybe a little. It's an eyesore, frankly. But do I march over there and tell him to put them away? Do I try to control him or his yard? Absolutely not. I just wave when I see him out getting his paper. It's his property, his business. Live and let live, that's my motto.

And it was the exact same way when I was working. When you're carrying the mail, you see all sorts of things. People's yards a mess, folks parking too close to the mailboxes, kids leaving their bicycles right in the middle of the sidewalk... you just step around it. You don't try to manage the whole neighborhood. And with my own kids, when my boys were growing up, my wife—Mary, God rest her—she used to say I was too lenient! If they wanted to paint their bedrooms some awful loud color, I'd just hand them the brush and say, "Don't drip on the carpet." You have to let people be. 

So, no, I don't have this... this urge to be the boss of everyone or dictate how a room is set up. I just like my own little personal space to be tidy. Which, again, doctor, just makes this whole community center thing so blasted confusing to me! That young volunteer, he was just doing his job, setting up for the luncheon, and it wasn't even my table! I wasn't in charge of the event! I was just there to have a sandwich and see my friends. So why I felt the need to suddenly march over there and try to control how he laid out that tablecloth... it's completely beyond me. It's like I lost my mind for a minute. But as a general rule? No. I don't need to control things. Not at all.
Have you ever found yourself repeating certain actions or rituals over and over?

Repeating things? Like... doing the exact same thing over and over? Well, no. No, I can't say I do. 

You see, doc, that goes right back to what I was saying earlier about efficiency. When you're a mail carrier for forty years, you learn a rule pretty quick, and the rule is: "Touch the mail once." You pick up a letter, you read the address, you slot it. If you're picking it up, putting it down, picking it up again to check the name, setting it aside... well, you're just wasting daylight, and you're never gonna finish your route before the streetlights come on. 

So I've always been a "do it once and do it right" kind of fellow. Take locking the front door at night. I told you about my deadbolt and chain. I slide the chain, I turn the bolt, I hear that heavy metal click, and that's it. I'm off to the bedroom. I don't stand there jiggling the doorknob for five minutes. I don't walk halfway down the hall, stop, and then turn around to go check it again. I know it's locked because I just locked it! My memory works just fine, thank the Lord. 

I actually knew a fella once, worked at the main sorting facility downtown—Frank, I think his name was, or maybe Fred... no, it was Frank. Anyway, Frank would check his car doors three, four, sometimes five times before he'd walk into the building for his shift. He'd walk away, turn around, pull the handle. Walk away, turn around, pull the handle. Used to drive us all absolutely crazy just watching him out the breakroom window. I never understood it. I asked him once, I said, "Frank, you locked it the first time, why are you going back?" And he just said he didn't feel right until he checked it again. 

I've never had that feeling. Once I do a thing, it's done. I wash my blue coffee cup, I dry it, I set it on the counter. I don't need to wash it twice. Which just... well, it just makes me sound like a very reasonable, practical man, doesn't it? A reasonable man who does things once and moves on with his life. And yet... there I was, making an absolute scene over a tablecloth that didn't even belong to me. It just doesn't fit! It's like you're talking to Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde here. I don't do rituals, I don't check things over and over, I'm as steady as a grandfather clock. So I just don't know, doctor. I really don't.
Do you feel uncomfortable or anxious when things are not symmetrical or perfectly aligned?

Symmetrical? You mean like... perfectly even on both sides, everything lined up just so? No, no, doctor. That's never been a concern of mine. 

If you came over to my house right now and looked down the main hallway, you'd see for yourself. My wife, Mary, she hung a whole gallery of family photos up there back in '98. Pictures of the boys, the grandkids, our trip to Mount Rushmore. And I swear to you, not a single one of those frames is level. They are staggered all over the place, a little crooked here, a little tilted there. Some folks might want to take a tape measure and a bubble level to them, make sure the gaps are exactly two inches apart all the way down, but me? I just like looking at the pictures. It doesn't bother me one bit that they aren't perfectly symmetrical. 

And it was the same way on the route. When you're bundling mail, you get all sorts of odd shapes. You get those big thick catalogs, little flimsy postcards, those square greeting cards that always cost extra postage... and when you wrap a rubber band around them, the edges stick out every which way. It's a mess, really. But if you stood at the back of the truck trying to make a perfectly neat, symmetrical stack out of everyone's mail, tapping the edges against the dashboard until they lined up? Well, like I said, you'd never get off the first block! You just bundle it up tight so nothing blows away, and you get walking. 

So no, things being a little off-center or asymmetrical doesn't make me anxious at all. It never has. Which is exactly why... I mean, I know I keep coming back to this, doctor, but it's the only thing on my mind. That tablecloth at the community center. It wasn't symmetrical. That young volunteer had it pulled way down on the left side, so it was pooling on the floor, and it was barely covering the edge of the table on the right. 

Now, like I just told you, normally I would walk right past a thing like that. I'd grab my ham and cheese on rye, pour a cup of decaf, and sit down with the boys. I wouldn't care one bit about an uneven tablecloth. But that day... I saw that crooked edge, and my heart just started hammering against my ribs. My hands started shaking, I started sweating, and I just started yelling at that poor kid. Over a tablecloth! A piece of cheap, thin plastic! I just... I don't understand why that one crooked thing made me feel like the world was caving in, when normally I wouldn't give a hoot. I keep trying to make sense of it, but I just can't.
Have you noticed any other situations, aside from the tablecloth incident, where you felt an overwhelming urge to correct or criticize someone?

Other situations? Well, no, that's just it, doctor. That's exactly why I'm sitting here in this chair right now, talking to you instead of being at the community center for the Tuesday morning cribbage game. It's just that one incident. 

I mean, I'm seventy-nine years old. I've lived a long time, seen a lot of things, dealt with a lot of people. And like I was saying before about my neighbor Bill and his trash cans, or the kids leaving their bikes out... I just don't get worked up over things like that. I'm a patient man. You have to be patient when you're a mail carrier, what with the dogs and the weather and the folks who want to stand on their porch and tell you their entire life story when you've still got three miles of walking to do. You just smile, nod, and keep moving. 

But that day at the center... I just don't know what came over me. I really don't. That poor young man, he was just volunteering his time, setting up the room for us seniors to have a nice luncheon, and I just... I completely blew up at him. I started yelling, raising my voice, making a whole scene in front of everyone. Over a crooked tablecloth! Can you imagine? An old man screaming at a teenager because a piece of plastic was hanging too low on one side. 

It was awful, doctor. Just awful. I could see the look on his face, he was so startled, and the other folks in the room, they all stopped talking and just stared at me. And the worst part is, I don't usually talk to people that way. I never have! Even when my boys were teenagers and they'd push my buttons, I never lost my temper like that. I might give them a stern look or tell them to go to their rooms, but I didn't scream at them. 

So when I realized what I had done, how I had acted... well, I was just so ashamed. I apologized, of course, but the damage was done. Everyone was looking at me like I was some crazy old man who'd finally lost his marbles. And honestly, for a minute there, I felt like I had. That's what brought me in here to see you. Because that kind of outburst, that... that aggression, I guess you could call it... it's just not me. It's not who I am. And the fact that it happened, and over something so trivial... it scares me, doctor. It really does. I just want to understand why I did it, so I can make sure it never, ever happens again. Because I can't be going around yelling at people over tablecloths. I just can't.
Have you ever felt like your attention to detail or need for order was interfering with your relationships or daily life?

Well, like I've been trying to explain, doctor, I really don't have this... this chronic need for order that you're talking about. I'm just not a fussy man, never have been. So it's not some lifelong obsession with details that's causing problems for me. 

But if you're asking if this whole... this whole situation, this feeling I've had since that day at the community center, if that is interfering with my daily life? Yes. Yes, it absolutely is. And it breaks my heart, it really does. 

Take the Día de los Muertos event, for example. Every year down at the center, we put on a big gathering. It's a beautiful thing. My wife, Mary—God rest her soul—she used to love it, and I've been helping organize the altars and coordinate the food for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now. Usually, I'm right in the thick of it. I'm the one making the phone calls, figuring out who is bringing the pan de muerto, who is picking up the marigolds from the florist on 4th Street, making sure we have enough folding chairs... it's a lot of work, but I've always enjoyed it. Keeps me busy. But lately... I just haven't been able to keep up with organizing it the way I usually do. I'll sit down at the kitchen table with my notepad and my rotary phone, and I just stare at the list of names. I can't bring myself to make the calls. I just don't have the focus, or the energy, and I feel terrible leaving the rest of the committee in the lurch, especially Rosa, since she's got that bad hip and shouldn't be doing all the running around. 

And it's not just the volunteer work, either. It's my friendships. I mentioned the Tuesday cribbage game earlier, didn't I? Well, I've stopped going to card nights altogether. We usually play on Tuesdays, and sometimes a few of us get together on Thursday evenings for a little penny poker. Just an excuse for us old-timers to get out of the house, chew the fat, maybe complain about our joints a little. But I haven't been since the tablecloth incident. 

I just... I don't feel steady around people right now. I'll be getting dressed to go, putting on my good shoes, and then my stomach just ties itself into a tight little knot. I start thinking, what if I snap again? What if someone deals the cards a little sloppy, or somebody spills a drop of coffee on the floor, and I just completely lose my mind over it the way I did with that poor volunteer? I can't risk making a fool of myself again. I can't risk treating my friends that way. So I just take my shoes off, sit in my armchair, and watch the television. It's lonely, doctor. It's terribly lonely. But I just don't trust myself right now, and it's throwing my whole life completely off track.
Have you been experiencing any intrusive thoughts or mental images that you feel compelled to repeat or act on?

Compelled to act on them? Well, no, I don't feel the need to do anything about them, like, you know, perform some kind of ritual or go out and do something crazy. I just want them to go away. But as for the thoughts and the images... yes. Yes, doctor, I have been having those. 

And it's not the tablecloth, if that's what you're wondering. It's... it's the other thing. The thing that started all this mess. 

I'll just be going about my day, doing absolutely nothing out of the ordinary. I could just be sitting at my kitchen table. It's a nice little table, right by the window so I can look out at the bird feeder in the backyard. My Mary, she always loved watching the cardinals out there in the mornings. Anyway, I'll be sitting right there, maybe working on the crossword puzzle from the Sunday paper, or having a piece of toast with marmalade, just completely minding my own business. And then... out of nowhere, I hear that man's rough voice in my head. 

It's so loud, doctor, and so real, it makes me jump in my seat like he's standing right there in the kitchen behind me. And if it's not that awful voice, it's the picture of it. I'll just suddenly see the donation envelope hitting the ground. Just... smacking against the concrete. I see it so vividly, the exact way it landed, the dirt on the ground, the way the light was hitting it... I see all of it, even when I'm just sitting at my kitchen table trying to figure out a five-letter word for 'sailboat'. 

I try to push it away, I really do. I'll shake my head, or I'll get up and go turn the radio on in the living room to try and drown it out. I'll try to find a baseball game, or maybe some classical music, just anything to fill my ears with something else. But it doesn't always work. That rough voice and that envelope falling... they just barge right into my mind whenever they please. It's like a movie I can't turn off, and I just have to sit there and wait for it to pass. It's exhausting, it really is.
Have you ever had any other episodes of intense anger or frustration that seemed out of character for you?

No, doctor, no. That's... well, like I was telling you at the very beginning of our chat today, that's exactly what brought me in here to see you in the first place. That one specific incident. Because blowing up at one of the younger volunteers over a crooked tablecloth... I mean, I just don't usually talk to people that way. I really don't. 

I've been trying to rack my brain ever since it happened, trying to think if I've ever flown off the handle like that before, and I just can't come up with a single time. My Mary, she always used to tell her friends that I was the most even-keeled man she'd ever met. And she was right! You know, when you're raising two boys, they test your patience. They really do. I remember when my oldest, Thomas, took the family station wagon out when he was sixteen and backed it right into the neighbor's brick mailbox. Scraped the whole side of the car, shattered the taillight. Was I upset? Of course I was. Money was tight back then. But did I scream at him? Did I make a scene? No, I sat him down at the kitchen table, we had a stern talk about responsibility, and he worked a summer job at the hardware store to pay for the repairs. Calm and collected. That's how I've handled things my whole life.

So to just completely lose my temper... to raise my voice at a boy who was just giving up his Saturday to help set up a luncheon for a bunch of old folks... it's completely out of character. It's like I was a different person for those few minutes. I can still see the way the plastic of that tablecloth was hanging off the edge of the folding table, just a few inches longer on the left side than the right. It was nothing! A gust of wind could have fixed it. But the anger that bubbled up inside me, it was so intense, so fast... it terrified me. That's why I'm sitting in this chair, doctor. Because I don't ever want to be the kind of man who talks to people that way, and I don't have any other history of acting like such a hothead. It's just this one, awful time.
Have you noticed any other times when you felt an overwhelming urge to correct or criticize someone, even if it wasn't as severe as the tablecloth incident?

Well, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor, no. Like I was just saying a moment ago, that's exactly what brought me in here to begin with. It really is just that one time. The fact that I blew up at one of the younger volunteers over a crooked tablecloth... well, it shook me, because I just don't usually talk to people that way. I really don't. 

You ask if there are other times, even minor ones, where I felt the urge to criticize, and I have to tell you, I'm just not a nitpicker. Never have been. When you work with volunteers for as long as I have down at the community center, you learn very quickly that you have to have a certain amount of grace. These aren't professionals, you know? They're just good, decent folks giving up their weekends to help out. If someone puts a fork on the wrong side of the plate, or if the coffee they brew is a little too weak, I just drink it and say thank you. I'd never dream of pulling someone aside to correct them over something so trivial. Life is too short to go around making people feel small. 

So no, I don't walk around with this... this urge to tell people they're doing things wrong. I don't have a critical bone in my body. That's why that afternoon was such a terrible shock to me. To just suddenly feel this overwhelming need to tear into that poor boy over a piece of cheap plastic hanging a little too far over the edge of a folding table... it was entirely out of the blue. I haven't felt anything like it before or since. But that one time... well, that one time was ugly enough to make me pick up the telephone and make this appointment.
Have you ever felt like you had to perform a specific task or ritual over and over to feel right or to calm your anxiety?

Well, like I touched on a little bit earlier when we were talking about those pictures in my head... no, I don't have anything like that. I don't feel any sort of urge to do something over and over again. 

I know the sort of thing you mean, though. My sister-in-law, Helen—God rest her soul—she was a terrible worrier. Whenever we'd all go out for Sunday dinner after church, she'd have to check the lock on her front door three or four times. She'd pull the handle, walk down the steps, turn right back around, and pull the handle again. Drove my brother Frank absolutely up the wall, let me tell you. But I've never been like that.

If you came over to my house right now and looked down the main hallway, you'd see for yourself. My wife, Mary, she hung a whole gallery of family photos up there back in '98. Pictures of the boys, the grandkids, our trip to Mount Rushmore. And I swear to you, not a single one of those frames is level. They are staggered all over the place, a little crooked here, a little tilted there. Some folks might want to take a tape measure and a bubble level to them, make sure the gaps are exactly two inches apart all the way down, but me? I just like looking at the pictures. It doesn't bother me one bit that they aren't perfectly symmetrical. 

And it was the same way on the route. When you're bundling mail, you get all sorts of odd shapes. You get those big thick catalogs, little flimsy postcards, those square greeting cards that always cost extra postage... and when you wrap a rubber band around them, the edges stick out every which way. It's a mess, really. But if you stood at the back of the truck trying to make a perfectly neat, symmetrical stack out of everyone's mail, tapping the edges against the dashboard until they lined up? Well, like I said, you'd never get off the first block! You just bundle it up tight so nothing blows away, and you get walking. 

So no, things being a little off-center or asymmetrical doesn't make me anxious at all. It never has. Which is exactly why... I mean, I know I keep coming back to this, doctor, but it's the only thing on my mind. That tablecloth at the community center. It wasn't symmetrical. That young volunteer had it pulled way down on the left side, so it was pooling on the floor, and it was barely covering the edge of the table on the right. 

Now, like I just told you, normally I would walk right past a thing like that. I'd grab my ham and cheese on rye, pour a cup of decaf, and sit down with the boys. I wouldn't care one bit about an uneven tablecloth. But that day... I saw that crooked edge, and my heart just started hammering against my ribs. My hands started shaking, I started sweating, and I just started yelling at that poor kid. Over a tablecloth! A piece of cheap, thin plastic! I just... I don't understand why that one crooked thing made me feel like the world was caving in, when normally I wouldn't give a hoot. I keep trying to make sense of it, but I just can't.

It was awful, doctor. Just awful. I could see the look on his face, he was so startled, and the other folks in the room, they all stopped talking and just stared at me. And the worst part is, I don't usually talk to people that way. I never have! Even when my boys were teenagers and they'd push my buttons, I never lost my temper like that. I might give them a stern look or tell them to go to their rooms, but I didn't scream at them. 

So when I realized what I had done, how I had acted... well, I was just so ashamed. I apologized, of course, but the damage was done. Everyone was looking at me like I was some crazy old man who'd finally lost his marbles. And honestly, for a minute there, I felt like I had. That's what brought me in here to see you. Because that kind of outburst, that... that aggression, I guess you could call it... it's just not me. It's not who I am. I can't risk making a fool of myself again. I can't risk treating my friends that way. So I just take my shoes off, sit in my armchair, and watch the television. It's lonely, doctor.
